title: Two sets of books — and what the restatement actually means
body:
## The restatement in plain language

On 13 May 2026, Sivers Semiconductors published its 2025 Annual Report — nearly three months after preliminary results had already circulated. The delay was not accidental. Embedded in the document was a disclosure that should arrest any investor treating the prior numbers as a baseline: a full PCAOB-aligned restatement of both FY2025 and FY2024, prepared as groundwork for a potential US dual listing. The effect was material. The EBIT loss for FY2025 widened by SEK 36.5 million. The net loss deepened by SEK 36.1 million. Book equity fell by SEK 127 million. And the FY2024 figures — already unattractive — were revised to look considerably worse.

Two sets of books now exist. Neither is wrong in a legal sense: Swedish K3 accounting, which Sivers has always reported under, permits practices that PCAOB does not. But for investors evaluating the company on a pre-listing basis, the PCAOB-restated figures are the ones that matter for comparability with US-listed peers. They are also the more conservative set.

| Metric | As Reported (K3) | PCAOB-Restated | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net Sales (SEK M) | 304.1 | 306.6 | +2.5 |
| EBIT (SEK M) | −141.3 | −177.8 | −36.5 |
| Net Result (SEK M) | −186.5 | −222.6 | −36.1 |
| EPS (SEK) | −0.69 | −0.81 | −0.12 |
| Equity (SEK M) | 1,076.8 | 949.8 | −127.0 |
| Equity/Share (SEK) | 3.46 | 3.05 | −0.41 |

*FY2025 — [Sivers 2025 Annual Report](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/)*

Revenue, curiously, moved slightly upward under PCAOB (SEK 304.1M → SEK 306.6M). That is not a comfort. It reflects the timing mechanics of the restatement: revenue was reallocated *out of* 2024 and *into* 2025, with some portion pushed further out to 2026 and beyond. Sivers' historical top line was worse than it appeared; its current period looks marginally better partly as an artifact of that reallocation.

## The five levers — and which one cuts deepest

The company disclosed five specific restatement drivers. Taken in order of analytical importance:

**Development capitalization impairment** is the most consequential. Swedish K3 accounting allows companies to capitalise R&D spending as a balance-sheet asset when commercial viability is assessed as probable. PCAOB applies a stricter standard: the threshold for recognising such capitalised costs is higher, and absent sufficient commercial evidence — signed volume commitments, for instance, rather than letters of intent — the asset must be expensed. Sivers had capitalised meaningful development expenditures under K3. The PCAOB restatement effectively says: not yet. The SEK 127-million reduction in book equity is the cumulative balance-sheet footprint of this reclassification. For a company whose equity coverage story depends heavily on the asset base supporting its laser platform, the haircut is not trivial.

**Revenue reallocation between periods** is conceptually simpler but historically damaging. Under PCAOB revenue recognition standards, certain contracts or milestone payments that K3 had recognised in FY2024 did not yet meet the criteria for recognition. The result is a FY2024 revenue revision from SEK 243.7M down to SEK 219.2M — a reduction of SEK 24.5 million, or roughly 10% of what was reported. More strikingly, the FY2024 net loss was revised from SEK 116.3M to SEK 183.9M — a SEK 67.6 million widening. Investors who benchmarked Sivers' loss trajectory against the K3 numbers have been working from a flattering baseline. The underlying deterioration in FY2024 was substantially larger than reported.

**Inventory revaluation** and **share-based compensation fair value updates** are more mechanical in nature. Inventory write-downs under PCAOB's lower-of-cost-or-net-realisable-value tests tend to be applied more conservatively than under K3; the fair value methodology for equity-settled awards follows US GAAP conventions that can produce different expense recognition patterns. Neither driver is unusual in a dual-listing restatement context. Both add to the cumulative EBIT drag.

**Income statement reclassification from by-nature to by-function** reshapes presentation rather than outcomes — R&D, COGS, and G&A are recut so US-style investors can read gross margin and operating leverage directly. This does not change the total loss, but it changes how analysts model it.

## What five years of growth actually looks like

Strip away the accounting complexity and the underlying trajectory is, at minimum, real. Revenue has grown at a 36.7% CAGR from 2016 to 2025, a roughly 16x expansion over the decade, per analyst estimates at [Global Equity Briefing](https://www.globalequitybriefing.com/p/sivers-semiconductors-hype-or-asymmetric). Free cash outflow has narrowed from SEK 151 million in FY2022 to SEK 66 million in FY2025. Operating margin improved from -83% (FY2022) to -39% (FY2025). The direction of travel is correct. The absolute level remains heavily negative.

Q4 FY2025 adds granularity. Standalone revenue of SEK 80.7M was up 5% year-on-year at reported rates, but 17% in constant currency — a meaningful divergence reflecting SEK appreciation. Product revenue of SEK 21.3M grew 13% quarter-on-quarter. Annualised from the Q4 run rate, revenue would be approximately SEK 320M — slightly below what the company's stated pipeline trajectory might suggest, but not inconsistent with a business in active customer qualification rather than high-volume production. The qualification-to-revenue lag in laser supply chains runs six to eighteen months from design-in to purchase order; Q4 product revenue is the seed of what may follow.

## Capital structure: the cost of survival

Sivers has funded its growth primarily through equity issuance. Since 2020, shares outstanding have increased by 101.58% — essentially, the share count doubled. Year-end FY2025 cash stood at SEK 43.5M against annual FCF consumption of SEK 66M: roughly three quarters of runway, give or take, before the next financing event.

The recent financing sequence tells its own story. A SEK 95M rights issue in 2025 diluted existing holders by approximately 8%. In February 2026, the company raised $17M via a term loan and convertible instrument — a structure that carries dilution optionality embedded in the convertible leg. In May 2026, it secured a $6.6M non-dilutive grant under the US Department of Defense's Microelectronics Commons NEMC Year 2 programme, earmarked for defence infrastructure modernisation. The grant is genuinely non-dilutive, but at current burn rates it covers roughly one quarter of FCF.

The June 15 Annual General Meeting will ask shareholders to authorise the issuance of up to 53,844,956 new shares — approximately 15% of current shares outstanding — covering warrants, convertibles, and any future ordinary share issuances. A separate proposal covers a 2% long-term incentive plan (approximately 7 million Class C options). Management has cited four stated uses: organic growth funding, potential M&A, strategic shareholder onboarding, and US listing enablement. A 15% authority does not compel immediate drawdown, but it sets the ceiling on what the board can issue before returning to shareholders. For a company that has doubled its share count in five years, any authorisation of this scope deserves scrutiny.

## The valuation arithmetic

At SEK 72.90 — a five-year high, touched during the research window — Sivers' market capitalisation is approximately SEK 22.7 billion, or roughly $2.2 billion at prevailing exchange rates. Against PCAOB-restated FY2025 revenue of SEK 306.6M, that is a price-to-sales multiple of approximately **74x**.

The substack analyst whose work informed this dossier constructed a bull-case 2030 model: 45% revenue CAGR, 25% operating margin, SEK 2.3 billion revenue, SEK 404 million net income. On those assumptions — which are generous — the analyst's implied fair value is SEK 14.52 per share. The current price is SEK 72.90: roughly five times that bull-case estimate.

The gap is not necessarily irrational in a market pricing optionality on co-packaged optics adoption. But it does mean the market is either assuming a considerably more aggressive ramp than the analyst's model, a higher terminal margin, or a non-trivial probability of acquisition at a strategic premium. It is not pricing a business at its operational fundamentals as they currently exist.

## The frame for what follows

The PCAOB restatement resolves one question and opens another. The resolved question is which set of numbers an investor should use: the restated figures are the right baseline, and they show a company that lost SEK 222.6M on SEK 306.6M of revenue in FY2025. The open question is whether the narrative that justifies SEK 22.7B in market capitalisation — CPO production beginning end-2026, a $453M pipeline growing 64% year-on-year, a US listing that re-rates the stock against American comparables — will be validated by shipped product and cash-generating customer ramps, or whether it will dissolve under the weight of further dilution, delayed qualification timelines, and a laser market that is less concentrated than the bull case assumes.

The financials show a company that is **real** — the growth is there, the margin improvement is there, the pipeline has names attached to it. They also show a company that is **under-funded** for the ambition it is selling — three quarters of cash, a 15% dilution proposal, and a convertible overhang. And they show a company valued for a scenario that has **not yet shipped**. The chapters that follow examine the technology, the customer ramps, and the competitive position to assess whether that gap closes — or widens.
